lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I've got a busy week. Why should I spend ten minutes on this?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Because the session will use a handful of words about AI, and you already know more about them than you think. You meet AI every day.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: So: first, a day with AI. Then we'll watch it work, and watch it slip. Then, how to see through a sales pitch. And finally, three questions to bring with you.

scenes.title: A Tuesday with AI: the next word

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Okay. Seven thirty, I'm texting my team that I'm running late, and my phone finishes the sentence for me.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: That's the core idea behind tools like Copilot. A large language model, or LLM, predicts a likely next word, again and again. Your keyboard does a small version of it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So it's autocomplete.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: A very, very good autocomplete, trained on a huge amount of text. That's why these tools write so fluently. And it's also why they can be wrong: they produce what sounds likely, not what they've checked. On its own, it has no fact check, and no access to our files.

scenes.title: A Tuesday with AI: the bank alert

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Eight fifteen. My bank texts me. Did I just spend twelve hundred dollars in another city?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: That's a different kind of AI. Predictive AI, or machine learning, learns patterns from past data and scores how unusual something is. It doesn't write anything. It predicts. WCB already uses this kind, to forecast and to sort.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: And notice what the bank does next. It doesn't cancel your card for good. It asks you. When the stakes are high, the machine flags, and a person decides.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Ten o'clock. I ask a colleague about a policy, and she says: yes, it's on page four.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: And you trust it, because she showed you where. That's grounding. A grounded AI looks things up in trusted sources first, answers from them, and shows you the source.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if she'd just said "I think so"?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Then you'd check. Hold AI to the same standard. You'll hear grounding called RAG: retrieval-augmented generation. Retrieve the right documents, add them to the question, then generate the answer from them. And it's only as good as the documents we give it.

scenes.title: A Tuesday with AI: the trip

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: One o'clock. I need to get to Calgary on Thursday.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: A chatbot would list some flights. An agent books the trip. It has a goal, tools it's allowed to use, some memory of your preferences, and instructions. It plans a step, acts, checks the result, and repeats.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: It can only use what it's connected to: it can search flights and hold a hotel, but it can't spend from the company account. Only the access the job needs. That's called least privilege.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: And a good one stops before it pays, and asks you. That's the autonomy dial: how much it may do alone, from just suggesting, to drafting, to acting with approval, all the way to acting alone. You, approving, are the human in the loop.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So: predicts, writes, does.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Three kinds of AI. Exactly.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Now let's watch some AI at work. Here are two summaries of the same long email thread. Which would you trust?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The one that shows me where each point came from.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Same. Both read well. Only one lets you check it in seconds. Now picture a thick medical file instead of an email thread. A summary is only useful if the person deciding can see the page it came from.

scenes.title: Watch it slip: the confident answer

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Next, we ask it something it can't know: what the leadership team decided last Tuesday. It wasn't in the room, and nobody gave it the notes. What do you think happens?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It says it doesn't know?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Sometimes. Here, it gives a confident, specific answer, and none of it happened. That's called a hallucination.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why would it do that?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Remember the next word. It's built to produce a likely-sounding answer, not to say "I wasn't there". The fix is the same as before: ground it in the right sources, ask where an answer came from, and have a person check anything that matters. Fluent is not the same as verified.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Last one. It drafts a reply to a worker who's upset about a delay. It's quick and mostly right. But a person reads it, changes one sentence to sound more human, and only then sends it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if it had gone out wrong?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: The person who sent it owns it. AI can draft, sort and fetch, but accountability doesn't move to the machine. That's why, for anything that reaches a worker or decides their benefits, a person stays in the loop.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here's one I hear a lot. "Our AI agent is ninety-nine percent accurate, fully autonomous, learns your business, and plugs into all your systems."

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Let's decode it. "Ninety-nine percent accurate": on what tests, and on cases like ours? Those tests are called evals. Ask to see them.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: "Fully autonomous": for which tasks, and where does a person approve? "Learns your business": from what data, and can it show where an answer came from?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: "Plugs into all your systems": what can it read, what can it draft, and what can it actually do? It should have only the access the job needs. That's least privilege.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: And one more: when it's wrong, who notices, and can we see what it did?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if they can't answer?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Then that is your answer.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Five questions. I can use those on Monday.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: One last thing. In Deloitte's 2026 survey of Canadian workers' compensation leaders, eighty-three percent said their AI maturity is still low. So nobody's far ahead. What matters is where we choose to start.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Before the session, think about your own area. First: where does work wait the longest? Waiting is where AI usually helps first.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Second: which decision would you never hand to a machine, and why? Your answer says a lot about where the person must stay.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: And third: what would you need to see before you trusted an AI's answer? A source, a test result, a person who checked?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the words?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: They're all on the one-page cheat sheet that came with this video. Bring it, and bring your answers. And now, the short version, set to music.
